passage:
"Tushar, stay back five minutes?"
"Did I mess up the client deck?"
"No. You fixed it." Omkar pulled up a chair. "The pricing slide. You caught the error I'd missed for two months."
"It was luck."
"It wasn't. So on tomorrow's call, you're presenting that part."
"Me? The client knows you."
"They'll know you too. I'll tell them it was your find." Omkar smiled. "Here's what took me three years to learn: always check the source sheet, not the summary. Now you know it in six months."
"Won't that make me... competition?"
"One day you'll probably run this team. Good. That's the point."
Next morning on the call, Omkar said, "Tushar found this, and he'll walk you through it," and muted himself.

qa.q: What error did Tushar catch?
qa.a: The error on the pricing slide that Omkar had missed for two months.

qa.q: What worry lies behind Tushar asking, "Won't that make me... competition?"
qa.a: He is worried Omkar might feel threatened, or that shining too brightly could cause trouble with his senior.

qa.q: What choice on the call shows Omkar mentoring without ego?
qa.a: He credited Tushar for the find in front of the client and muted himself so Tushar could present, sharing the spotlight instead of keeping it.

qa.q: How might the client see Tushar after the call?
qa.a: They'd likely see him as capable and trusted by his senior, which builds his reputation early.

passage: When Sunaina joined our newsroom as a trainee two years ago, she couldn't write a headline under twelve words. I, Nandini, was only three years ahead of her and the only other woman on the desk, and I taught her everything I had been slow to learn: cut the first paragraph, call the second source, never trust a press note. In monthly meetings I made a point of saying which stories were her ideas. Last week she got the national desk job. I had applied too. For about an hour I sat in the washroom with a hot sting in my chest. Then I remembered her first story, on the bus depot strike, and how she had rewritten it four times. I went out and hugged her. My editor asked if I was okay. I was. What I gave her was never mine to keep.

qa.q: Which job did Sunaina get last week?
qa.a: The national desk job.

qa.q: What did Nandini feel in the washroom, and what changed it?
qa.a: She felt a hot sting at being passed over, but remembering how hard Sunaina worked on her first story turned it into pride.

qa.q: How did Nandini make sure Sunaina got credit along the way?
qa.a: In monthly meetings she pointed out which stories were Sunaina's ideas instead of letting them blend into her own.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel when Nandini hugs her?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel relieved and deeply grateful, knowing her mentor is glad rather than resentful 🤍

Team lead's observation note, design studio. Vandana.
Payal (25) has been guiding our intern, Bilal. In week one she showed him her file-naming system and shortcut sheet, sat with him through two client reviews, and let him make the mistakes she could have prevented, then talked them over afterwards. At Friday's all-hands, when the bakery logo was praised, she said, "That's Bilal's concept. I only helped with the colours." Bilal now designs faster than she does on some tasks. When I mentioned this, she said, "Good, then I can learn his tricks." Next: I'm recommending Payal for the mentor programme, and Bilal will lead the next small brief with her as reviewer.

qa.a: "That's Bilal's concept. I only helped with the colours."

qa.q: What does Payal's reply "Good, then I can learn his tricks" show about how she feels?
qa.a: She feels glad rather than threatened that Bilal is faster, and is open to learning from him.

qa.q: Why did letting Bilal make mistakes and talking them over later work well?
qa.a: He learned by doing and understood why, which builds real skill instead of dependence on Payal.

qa.q: How might Bilal feel hearing his name credited at the all-hands?
qa.a: He'd likely feel proud and seen, and more confident to lead the next brief.

passage:
Friday night
Staff meeting today. The district office praised our Class 6 fractions results, and the principal turned to me, since I'm the senior maths teacher. I said, "The sweet-shop project was Pema's idea. She designed the price tags, the pretend money, all of it. I only helped with the worksheets." Pema went red and stared into her tea.
Honestly, a small voice wanted the credit. I'm twenty-six, and it was my first real praise too. But I watched Pema teach that lesson, and it was better than anything I'd have managed at her stage. Maybe better than mine now.
I spent her first year showing her how to handle a noisy room and mark faster. Now she's teaching me things. That's how it should go. She'll outgrow me by next year, and I'm fine with that. Mostly.
Ira

qa.q: Whose idea was the sweet-shop project?
qa.a: It was Pema's idea.

qa.q: What does Ira's admission about 'a small voice' wanting the credit show?
qa.a: Ira was tempted to keep the praise, hungry for recognition at twenty-six, but chose to give it to Pema anyway.

qa.q: Which choice in the staff meeting mattered most for Pema, and why?
qa.a: Ira naming Pema publicly as the designer, which gives Pema confidence and a reputation of her own.

qa.q: What might Pema feel as she goes red and stares into her tea?
qa.a: She may feel shy but proud, and surprised that her mentor gave her the credit in front of everyone.

passage: In the Marathwada village where Lokesh worked as a farm adviser, he had spent a year teaching Ramesh, the new junior, everything: soil testing, how to talk to proud old farmers, how to listen longer than you speak. Now Ramesh had tried something Lokesh never had: a drip-line trial on Kailash-kaka's field, and it had worked. At the gram sabha meeting, the sarpanch thanked "Lokesh-saheb's team." Lokesh stood up. "This was Ramesh's idea, all of it. He should explain it." Ramesh went red and started talking, then got confident. Soon farmers were asking him questions, not Lokesh. Lokesh felt a small pinch, watching them turn away from him. Then he felt something bigger: pride. He'd taught Ramesh to listen. Ramesh had taught himself the rest. That was how it was supposed to go.

passage: Sami had worked at the little Osaka bakery for four years before Hiroshi arrived, all elbows and nerves. Sami showed him everything: how to read dough by touch, when to open the oven, how to apologise to customers in the right tone. In spring Hiroshi tried a yuzu bun of his own. It sold out by ten every morning, faster than anything Sami had ever made. When a food writer visited and asked who created it, the owner looked at Sami. Sami shook his head and pointed. "Hiroshi. It's his." Later, closing up, Hiroshi said, "You could have said it was yours. You taught me." Sami shrugged, feeling a flicker of envy, then warmth. "I taught you dough. You made the bun." He tied his apron tighter. Soon Hiroshi would probably open his own place. Sami hoped he would.

qa.q: By what time did the yuzu bun sell out each morning?
qa.a: It sold out by ten every morning.

qa.q: What did Sami feel when Hiroshi said "You could have said it was yours"?
qa.a: Sami felt a flicker of envy, then warmth and pride in Hiroshi's success.

qa.q: What does Sami's answer to the food writer show about good mentoring?
qa.a: By pointing to Hiroshi and saying "It's his," Sami gave public credit, putting Hiroshi's growth above his own recognition.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi see Sami after that visit?
qa.a: Hiroshi seems grateful and surprised, recognising how much Sami gave up by crediting him, which may deepen his trust.

passage: At the Mumbai swimming club, Zubin had coached the under-12s for three years before Wasim joined as his assistant. Zubin shared his drills, his notebook of every child's quirks, even the trick for calming kids who froze before a race. By December Wasim had redesigned the kick sets, and two of his swimmers made the state team. At the annual meeting, the club secretary said, "Great work, Zubin." Zubin took the mic. "Those two were Wasim's. His plan, his mornings. I just held the stopwatch." Wasim stared at the floor. Afterwards the secretary asked if Wasim could take the senior squad next year, above Zubin. Zubin felt his stomach drop for a second. Then he nodded. "He's ready." Driving home, he smiled, a bit sore, a bit proud, and glad he'd got to see someone grow.

qa.q: How many of Wasim's swimmers made the state team?
qa.a: Two of Wasim's swimmers made the state team.

qa.q: How did Zubin feel when the secretary suggested Wasim take the senior squad?
qa.a: Zubin's stomach dropped for a second, and he felt sore but also proud and glad.

qa.q: Which choice at the annual meeting showed mentoring without ego, and why?
qa.a: He took the mic and publicly credited Wasim, refusing praise for work that wasn't his.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel when Zubin said "He's ready"?
qa.a: Wasim would likely feel valued and trusted, though perhaps also awkward about stepping above his mentor.

passage:
Dear Sachin,
I wanted to write this before the team meeting tomorrow, where I'll say it publicly too.
When you joined last year, I taught you everything I knew about the audit software. You picked it up faster than I did. Then you went further. The automation you built for the monthly reports saves us twenty hours a month.
Some people have asked if I feel threatened that you've outgrown what I taught. Honestly, for a day, I did. Then I felt proud. That's what teaching is for.
Tomorrow I'll tell the whole team the automation was your idea. It was.
Keep going. Outgrow me more.
Pooja

passage:
I'm Jeevan, and Sharmila was my first mentor at the architecture firm. I can't say what she really thought, but I can tell you what she did.
She taught me everything: drawing software, client meetings, site visits. She let me make mistakes and fix them.
Last spring I designed a school building that won a small award. At the ceremony, Sharmila could have said, "My team's work." Instead she stood up and said, "This is Jeevan's design. I only helped at the start."
Later I got an offer from a bigger firm. I was scared to tell her. When I did, she smiled and said, "Go. You've outgrown us. That's good."
She still sends me articles sometimes. She never asks for credit.

qa.q: What did Jeevan design that won an award?
qa.a: A school building.

qa.q: What might Sharmila's smile when Jeevan left suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and happy for Jeevan, not threatened by being outgrown.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's choices show mentoring without ego?
qa.a: Teaching everything, letting Jeevan fix mistakes, crediting the design publicly, and encouraging Jeevan to move on.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel about telling Sharmila about the offer?
qa.a: Jeevan felt scared to tell her, worried how she'd react.

passage: Kamal, you're worried the new boy you're training will overtake you. Let me tell you about Harpreet. I was twenty-five, a sub-editor at the Chandigarh paper, and they gave me this nervous kid straight from journalism school. I taught him everything: how to cut a story without killing it, how to call a source back. His first front-page piece was half my rewrite, but I put only his name on it. Four years later, he became my boss. My boss! I sulked for exactly one evening. Then I went in the next morning and said, 'Congratulations, Harpreet. Don't forget to cut the adjectives.' He laughed. He still sends me his big stories before print: 'Gurleen Didi, read this first.' That's the best thing I ever grew, beta. It wasn't mine to keep.

qa.q: Where did Gurleen work at twenty-five?
qa.a: As a sub-editor at the Chandigarh paper.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when Harpreet became her boss?
qa.a: She felt hurt and sulky for one evening before choosing to be generous.

qa.q: Gurleen put only Harpreet's name on his first front-page piece. Why was that a good choice?
qa.a: It gave him the confidence of owning the work and showed she cared about his growth more than her own credit.

qa.q: How might Harpreet feel about Gurleen now?
qa.a: Harpreet clearly trusts and respects her, still sending his big stories to her first.

In the meeting, when the client praised the booking flow, Chinmay said, 'That's Vandana's design. She'll walk you through it.' Afterwards his manager said, 'You could have presented it yourself.' Chinmay shrugged. 'She's going to be better than me. I'd like to have helped with that.'

passage: In the Hyderabad design studio, Devika had spent six months showing Shankar, the new junior, everything she had learned the hard way: how to talk to clients who say "make it pop", how to name files so nobody panics later.
